fatal_errors: The target material is an as-cast dual-phase FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, whereas the generated hypothesis assumes a generic single-phase solid solution.
The governing intervention—aging between approximately 550 and 750°C—is replaced by composition changes, so the proposed experiment cannot reconstruct the thermal embrittlement and recovery behavior.
The hypothesis omits the central L12-ordering and jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary mechanism, including elevated APBE, inhibited cross-slip, planar slip, and phase-boundary-tip stress concentration.
The cited evidence supports lattice-distortion strengthening and, in places, improved ductility; it does not support the key assertion that excessive distortion causes brittle fracture.
Changing composition to vary lattice distortion also changes phase stability, chemistry, modulus, and strengthening mechanisms, preventing a controlled attribution to lattice distortion.
explanation: The response addresses the broad topic of HEA brittleness and proposes a testable tensile series, but it does not recover the target material, treatment, temperature window, structural mediators, or ductile-brittle-ductile outcome. The target predicts minimum ductility after roughly 600°C aging and recovery near 750°C due to changes in L12 ordering and FCC/B2 boundary structure. In contrast, the generated hypothesis proposes a generic optimum versus composition-controlled lattice distortion at room temperature and gives no quantitative service boundary. Its falsification rule merely negates the main assertion and lacks discriminating microscopy of dislocation pile-ups and crack initiation at jagged phase-boundary tips or tests excluding impurity segregation. Most importantly, the supplied evidence establishes that lattice distortion can alter dislocation behavior and improve strength and ductility, but does not validate the proposed excessive-distortion embrittlement threshold.
